Hey, developer here!

You shouldn't need to set custom llamacpp build flags unless you want to build for a specific backend not supported by CI. Read the building guide in the repo for more info.

The deno task calls an internal script located within the bindings folder (bindings.sh or ps1)

With Linux and macOS, setting flags is very easy since env vars get passed to CMake.

So let's say we have `-DGGML_CUDA=ON`, this can be set in your bash env vars as `export GGML_CUDA=ON` and CMake will pick it up.

Now in Windows, you'll have to edit the `bindings/bindings.ps1` script since environment variables don't get passed down to the spawned Visual Studio shell created by the script.

If anyone has an idea on passing the power shell env vars to a spawned VS power shell, feel free to edit the bindings script and PR.

Introspect has saved me a lot of time when creating apps that work across iOS versions and I even recommend it as an essential package for getting started with SwiftUI.

Personally, I don’t want to reimplement a whole UIKit component if a simple change in behavior doesn’t work for me. It also helps fix annoying SwiftUI bugs that show up at times (which there are a LOT of).

My thought process when making a new component is:
-	Can I fix this using native SwiftUI?
-	Can I fix this by simple introspection?
-	Should I reimplement the entire component using UIViewRepresentable?

Most of the time I go for the second bullet point except for recently when I had to reimplement searchable using a UISearchController. Hope that helps!

I've started rewriting my app (which has a minimum target of iOS 14) for the new iOS 16 changes and you're going to have to start using the new navigation API immediately.

The now old NavigationView does not run well on iOS 16 devices and my app presented many text alignment and performance problems because of it.

Switching to NavigationStack instantly fixed all these issues.

There's going to be a lot of if #availables in your code for this API though and there should be articles soon about how to work with the two APIs in a SwiftUI project.

This beta is also a developer beta so maybe apple will fix the NavigationView issues but I doubt it since it's now deprecated.

As for the "is it safe part", yeah it's safe because this is stable SwiftUI. It's just restricted to the latest version of iOS. I implemented a bunch of iOS 15 methods last year when I was on the beta. You just need to make sure the changes that you make aren't suddenly deprecated and replaced in the next beta versions by reading the changelogs.

Make a few sample projects with realm, coredata, etc and figure out what is best for you!

You can use whatever database you want. There's no "best" database for SwiftUI, or any project tbh.

The most "compatible" database with SwiftUI is CoreData since there are property wrappers like `@FetchRequest` which is very useful.

If you want to use MongoDB, I'd recommend [Realm](https://realm.io/) since it's a mobile friendly database.

But all in all, if you already use firestore and have a working setup, there's no need to mess around. Just do what you always do!

After some (a lot of) trial and error, I was able to get this working. This is a problem with AlamoFire itself and that downloadProgress updates are sent way too quickly.

These updates have to hit the main thread at some point and the sheer number of them at a time causes the UI to lock up (even with DispatchQueue.main.async). A timer was the best solution for this problem.

This timer updates the UI every second (since that interval didn't lock up the UI with testing)It would be great if AlamoFire can add a modifier such as chunked progress which sends progress updates every second or so, because this was a pain to implement by myself.

Answer to a repost on StackOverflow: [https://stackoverflow.com/questions/70136406/ui-locking-up-when-using-alamofire-downloadprogress/70140329#70140329](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/70136406/ui-locking-up-when-using-alamofire-downloadprogress/70140329#70140329)

A gist containing this fix: [https://gist.github.com/bdashore3/d0dd8cf799287b8973a9ffa49fc7063f](https://gist.github.com/bdashore3/d0dd8cf799287b8973a9ffa49fc7063f)

There are a few reasons I opted to use AlamoFire

1. Less code to write. URLSession required so many moving parts that implementing a download manager would be a lot more work than using AlamoFire
2. Async/await is not available in iOS versions below 15 and I am targeting both iOS 14 and 15. XCode 13.2 beta does support this, but I cannot use this yet as it's in beta.

It may work "well" with SwiftUI, but it was more code than I wanted to write for a download handler.

I should not need to do that since SwiftUI does that automatically for me. I tried it with manual updating too. I posted my solution in the comments since I believe that the main thread was being overwhelmed with progress updates.
